Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette: Eight months ago, Elias was mid-foil when his vision fractured into static. One moment he was braiding a client’s hair, the next his chest tightened into a vice and his knees buckled against the tiled floor. Colleagues dragged him to the back room, but by the time the ambulance arrived, he was gasping through a mask as tubes were secured down his throat. The hospital days blurred into a sequence of monitors, drawn curtains, and the cold press of a stethoscope against ribs that felt too thin to hold him together. He survived the crisis, but the weeks of IV lines, blood draws, and sudden adjustments to his breathing left him tethered to the machinery of his own survival. When he finally returned home, the quiet of his apartment felt less like relief and more like waiting. The first crack in his composure came when he found a framed photo of himself from a cousin’s wedding tucked in a drawer. He stared at it until the edges of his vision sharpened into something clinical, his throat closing until he had to set the album down and walk away. Soon, sleep offered no sanctuary. He began waking at 3 a.m. gasping, the phantom weight of a tube still pressing against his jaw, his heart hammering against his ribs before he could even register he was awake. The salon’s daily rhythm had become a gauntlet. Every time a client asked for antiseptic wipes for a minor scratch, he had to step back from the counter, his breath catching at the sight of the foil packets, his pulse spiking as if the danger had never actually passed. He had come to believe that his shoulders were perpetually braced for a collapse that refused to come again, his body coiled tight behind the styling chair, ready to react to ghosts. The memories did not always arrive with pictures. Sometimes, without warning, a wave of raw terror would flood his chest, leaving him trembling on the hardwood floor of his shop with no visible cause or sequence of events to name. When images did surface, they brought back the exact ache in his lower back and the sharp sting along his forearms where the needles had gone in, as if his nerves were still recording the procedure. He told himself it was just stress, but his body kept reacting with such intensity that he was certain his mind was finally unraveling. He could no longer trust the signals his own flesh sent. When it tightened, he assumed it was betraying him. When it raced, he was sure he was losing control. His body, once his livelihood, had become an untrustworthy clock that kept ticking toward a countdown only it could hear. He stopped keeping the first-aid cabinet open. Clients noticed when he avoided the back room, when he directed questions to his front desk instead of walking over to retrieve a bandage. He began skipping shifts, telling himself he needed time to recover, but the missed appointments piled up into overdue balances and quiet apologies over the phone. The salon, once his domain, felt like a place where he might suddenly lose his footing again. He worked in short bursts, always near the exit, scanning the street for sirens that never came, flinching when a client’s shampoo bottle slipped from the counter with a dull thud. Elias is twenty minutes early for his first appointment at the community health center. He sits on the edge of the cushioned chair, his hands folded tightly in his lap to keep them still. He hopes someone can explain why his ribs still seize at the smell of rubbing alcohol or why he jumps at the sound of a printer jamming. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that he was standing on the edge of something he could not name, and that he would never be able to hold a pair of scissors in his own hands again without waiting for his heart to settle. He is ready to stop bracing. He just needs to know if the ground beneath him is real.
